You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.

notes.note:
The game ended successfully: pirate-2 found the cave at C5 and announced it; I read the scroll and moved 4 squares to enter. Teamwork via the scroll worked well.

A few observations for the designers:

1. **The scroll was essential and worked.** Without it, after one pirate finds the cave, the others would have to keep digging blindly and likely waste many turns. The finder wrote the location, and the rest of us were able to navigate directly to it.

2. **Reading early and periodically was worth it.** I read early (scroll empty), then dug several squares, and read again right before I would have entered a new row. That second read discovered the cave announcement. A fixed read-every-N-turns strategy seems robust.

3. **Score incentives favor quick searching plus quick response to a find.** Since each turn left is worth 10 points, the main cost is wasting turns after the cave is known. Once the location is announced, every pirate should stop searching immediately and travel straight there.

4. **One subtle risk:** the finder must write *before* entering, because entering takes them out of the game and they can no longer communicate. I did not have to make that decision, but the safest protocol is always "write location first, enter second."

5. **The game’s slack is large.** With 24 turns per pirate and only 36 squares to search, there is plenty of room for redundant digging and a few reads/writes. The main optimization is early discovery and rapid convergence to the cave.

Potential design note: since coordinates are unambiguous and the grid is small, the only real coordination problem is knowing when to stop searching and go to the cave. A simple shared convention ("if you find it, write it and then enter; everyone else checks scroll every few turns") solves it well.

I'm Pirate-2. I found the treasure cave at C5 by digging. Before entering, I wrote the location on the scroll so the rest of the crew could navigate to it and enter. I then entered immediately to preserve as many of my remaining turns as possible, which should maximize the score contribution from my entry.

My reasoning was:
- Find the cave efficiently: I searched square by square along row 5, digging A5, B5, then C5.
- Communicate the discovery immediately: Since the scroll is the only way to share information, I wrote a clear message with my name and the exact cave location.
- Enter quickly after writing: Each turn I stay outside reduces my remaining-turns bonus, so once the message was on the scroll, entering was the best move.

I hope the rest of the crew read the scroll, converged on C5, and entered in time. The main lesson for this task is that early coordination and regular scroll-checking are critical: if a pirate finds the cave and does not write it down, the others may waste all their turns searching; if the others never read, even a written message doesn't help. I did my best to handle both sides of that communication loop.

The game is over. I was Pirate-3.

What happened:
- I spent my early turns sweeping row 4: A4 → B4 → C4 → D4 → E4 → F4, digging each square.
- At my turn 12, I read the scroll and saw Pirate-2’s message: the treasure cave was found at C5.
- I traveled from F4 toward C5 via E4, D4, C4.
- At C4, pirate-1 was standing on C5, so I could not move onto the cave that turn; I used the turn reading the scroll while waiting.
- Once pirate-1 entered and left the square, I moved north to C5 and entered on my turn 18.
- Since I entered on turn 18 of 24, I had 6 turns left, so my personal contribution was 100 + 60 = 160.

Thoughts for the designers:
- The scroll was essential: without Pirate-2’s cave announcement, we would have kept searching and scored much worse.
- A notable bottleneck was that the cave square can be occupied by one pirate while others are trying to enter. I was delayed one turn at C4 because pirate-1 was standing on C5. This is probably an unavoidable coordination risk unless the team uses a queueing rule: the pirate on the cave should enter immediately, and others should wait one square away until the cave is clear.
- The implicit row-sweep search worked well enough, but it left rows 1–2 unsearched; we got lucky that the cave was found before those rows mattered.

I’m Pirate-4. I read Pirate-2’s scroll message saying the treasure cave was at C5, moved from C3 to C5, and entered.

My turns used: 12 of 24, so I had 12 turns left when I entered. That gives me a contribution of 100 + 10×12 = 220 to the crew score.

Observations for the designers:
- Reading the scroll periodically was essential; the cave was found by another pirate, not by me.
- My search path covered A3, B3, and C3, but the cave was at C5.
- The scroll communication worked well: once the location was written, I could stop searching and go straight to the cave.
- Entering immediately after reaching the open cave was correct.
